**(Travel + Leisure)** — It’s no surprise that Americans have strong opinions—especially about the cities they call home and the places they visit.

In fact, those feelings are so strong that, in the 2008 *America’s Favorite Cities* survey—conducted by travelandleisure.com and CNN Headline News—Americans cast more than 600,000 votes on 45 characteristics across 25 cities. They weighed in on everything from shopping, food, culture, and nightlife to cleanliness and affordability. New Orleans earned the No. 1 rankings for fine dining and live music.

In 2007, cities that claimed the top spots had plenty to celebrate, including Chicago, Illinois, for dining and Austin, Texas, for the best singles scene. But there were also plenty of upsets—or upset people, that is. After all, someone had to finish last.

Unfortunately for the proud residents of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, America ranked their city dead last in the attractive-people category. Meanwhile, Los Angeles, California, took the title of least friendly city—a distinction many had expected New York City to claim.

### Notable Changes

The 2008 results brought several surprises. New Orleans, Louisiana, edged out New York as the best city for fine dining. Las Vegas, Nevada, claimed the No. 1 spot for the best singles scene, while former leader Austin fell to No. 5. In the cleanliness category, Portland, Oregon, displaced Minneapolis, Minnesota, from first place.

See all the *America’s Favorite Cities* results—and play the new AFC game, *What’s YOUR Fave?*

Other cities, however, maintained their dominant positions. New York retained its No. 1 ranking as the country’s best destination for people-watching, while Charleston, South Carolina, was once again voted America’s friendliest city.

### Find Your Vacation

There is plenty more to explore beyond the rankings. If you are looking for a great destination, the Vacation Finder at travelandleisure.com can help you find the ideal city for your interests.

Austin and New Orleans, for example, are lively destinations for live music, inexpensive ethnic food, and vintage shopping. If you prefer something more high-minded, consider Washington, D.C., which ranks No. 1 for museums, or New York, which ranks No. 1 for classical music.

Travelers seeking urban sophistication paired with the exhilaration of the outdoors should head to Honolulu, Hawaii—No. 1 for active and adventure vacations—Portland, No. 1 for public parks and access to the outdoors, or Denver, Colorado, No. 1 for athletic and active residents.

If you are planning a trip with children, Orlando, Florida, remains the top choice, though alternatives such as San Diego, California, and Washington, D.C., also rate highly among travelers.

Those seeking a romantic getaway should try their luck in Honolulu, Charleston, or San Francisco, California, each of which offers its own distinctive charms.

And what happened at the bottom of the rankings? Did Philadelphia rally voters and climb the attractiveness scale? Did Angelenos take the criticism about being the least friendly to heart and begin offering fellow freeway drivers a kinder, gentler salute?

Read on to find out.

Here are the **top three cities »** in several categories, as selected by visitors. Visit travelandleisure.com for the complete results—best and worst—for every city and category, as ranked by both residents and visitors.

### “What’s YOUR Fave?”

You have voted on the characteristics of your favorite cities, but which one is America’s favorite city overall? Tell us.

## America’s Favorite Cities in 2008

The 2008 America’s Favorite Cities survey offered a wide-ranging look at how travelers and residents perceived 25 major U.S. destinations. More than 600,000 votes were cast across 45 categories covering nearly every aspect of urban life, from dining, nightlife, and cultural attractions to cleanliness, affordability, and the character of local residents.

Several cities reinforced their long-standing reputations. New Orleans ranked first for both fine dining and live music, reflecting the city’s celebrated culinary traditions and deep musical heritage. Its restaurants, jazz clubs, and lively entertainment districts continued to distinguish it as one of the country’s most culturally vibrant destinations.

Las Vegas led the survey’s singles scene, supported by its abundance of nightclubs, casinos, shows, and late-night entertainment. Portland, meanwhile, earned recognition as the cleanest city among those surveyed, strengthening its image as an environmentally conscious and well-maintained urban center.

Other familiar favorites held on to their leading positions. New York remained the top city for people-watching, thanks to the extraordinary variety of residents and visitors found on its streets, in its parks, and throughout its public spaces. Charleston once again ranked highest for friendliness, confirming the South Carolina city’s reputation for hospitality and warmth.

Taken together, the results showed both change and continuity in the way Americans viewed their cities. Some destinations gained attention for evolving food, entertainment, or lifestyle scenes, while others remained closely associated with qualities they had embodied for years. The survey ultimately demonstrated that a city’s appeal rests not only on its attractions, but also on its atmosphere, affordability, cleanliness, culture, and people.

### Travel and Leisure in American Life

Travel and leisure play an important role in the lives of many Americans. Vacations offer a chance to escape daily routines, spend time with family and friends, and discover new places. From weekend road trips to international journeys, Americans travel for relaxation, adventure, culture, and personal growth.

Domestic travel is especially popular because the United States offers a wide variety of destinations. Travelers can visit national parks, explore major cities, relax on beaches, or enjoy small towns and historic sites. Road trips remain a favorite tradition, giving people the freedom to travel at their own pace. Camping, hiking, theme parks, and visits to relatives are also common leisure activities.

International travel has become increasingly appealing as Americans seek new experiences and cultural connections. However, cost, limited vacation time, and work responsibilities can influence how often people travel. As a result, short trips, “staycations,” and budget-friendly vacations have gained popularity.

Whether traveling far from home or enjoying leisure activities nearby, Americans often see free time as an opportunity to recharge. Travel can create lasting memories, strengthen relationships, and provide a broader understanding of the world.

counterfactuals.output:
# Familiar Favorites Hold Their Ground in Travel + Leisure’s 2008 City Survey

**New York remained the country’s capital of shopping and style, Miami again stood out for attractive residents, and Charleston preserved its reputation for hospitality in Travel + Leisure’s 2008 America’s Favorite Cities survey.**

The annual poll asked readers and other travelers to rate 25 major U.S. destinations across dozens of categories, including food, culture, nightlife, shopping, weather and the character of local residents. Rather than naming one overall “best city,” the survey produced separate rankings for each attribute.

The 2008 results showed more continuity than upheaval compared with the previous year. New York again dominated urban categories such as shopping, fashion, theater and people-watching, reinforcing its strong performance in the 2007 survey. Its crowds, expense and pace, however, continued to keep it from scoring as highly in relaxation and value.

Miami repeated as the city with the country’s most attractive residents, with San Diego also placing near the top. New Yorkers were again regarded as especially stylish, while Charleston remained a leader for friendly people. As in 2007, the findings demonstrated that travelers drew a distinction between cities they considered glamorous and those they found welcoming.

Several regional favorites also held on to their specialties. Austin remained closely associated with live music, while New Orleans scored strongly for music, nightlife and distinctive local food. The Crescent City’s showing was particularly notable as tourism continued to recover after Hurricane Katrina. Honolulu again benefited from its weather and appeal as a relaxing escape, and San Francisco remained a favorite for scenery, dining and cultural attractions.

Washington performed well for museums, monuments and history, while Chicago’s architecture, skyline and big-city dining helped keep it among the survey’s leading cultural destinations. Western cities generally fared better in outdoor recreation, weather and active lifestyles than their older East Coast counterparts.

At the other end of the lighter, people-focused rankings, Philadelphia once more received low marks for the attractiveness and style of its residents—a repeat of one of the most publicized results from 2007. Such findings were based on respondents’ impressions, however, rather than objective measures.

The year-to-year comparison suggested that city reputations changed slowly. The same destinations largely continued to “own” the categories most closely tied to their public images: New York for fashion and shopping, Miami for looks, Charleston for friendliness, Austin for music, New Orleans for nightlife and Honolulu for relaxation.

Travel + Leisure’s survey was not a scientific assessment of municipal performance. Respondents chose which cities to rate, and residents and visitors could view the same destination differently. Still, the 2008 edition offered a snapshot of how American travelers saw the country’s major cities—and showed that, at least compared with 2007, familiar reputations remained remarkably durable.

counterfactuals.output:
# America’s favorite cities: 600,000 votes, 25 urban personalities

*Travel + Leisure’s 2008 America’s Favorite Cities survey asked residents and visitors to judge 25 destinations on everything from food and culture to nightlife, friendliness and romance. The result was less a single “best city” than a guide to finding the right city for every kind of trip.*

More than 600,000 votes helped shape the 2008 rankings, turning familiar rivalries—New York versus Chicago, Austin versus Nashville, Honolulu versus San Diego—into a broad snapshot of how travelers experienced urban America.

Participants rated 25 cities across dozens of categories, including restaurants, shopping, museums, live music, outdoor recreation, family appeal and quality of life. Residents could assess their hometowns, while visitors supplied an outsider’s perspective. Those responses were then compiled into category rankings.

The survey was a reader poll, not a scientific measure of population or tourism performance. Cities with enthusiastic local followings could benefit, while personal experience inevitably influenced the results. Still, the volume of voting revealed something useful: Different cities excel for very different reasons.

New York’s cultural reach, Austin’s music scene, Orlando’s family attractions and Honolulu’s mix of scenery and leisure cannot be reduced to one overall score. The real value of the rankings is in matching a destination to the traveler.

## For music: Austin, Nashville and New Orleans

**Austin, Texas**  
The “Live Music Capital of the World” offers clubs and concert rooms well beyond the festivals that made it famous. Travelers can move from country and blues to indie rock and Latin music in a single evening, particularly around downtown, East Austin and South Congress.

**Nashville, Tennessee**  
Country music remains the headline, but Nashville’s appeal extends from the honky-tonks of Lower Broadway to the songwriting rooms and studios of Music Row. The Country Music Hall of Fame and the Grand Ole Opry add historical depth.

**New Orleans, Louisiana**  
Music here is woven into everyday life. Jazz clubs, brass bands, neighborhood bars and street performances make New Orleans a destination where the soundtrack is as important as the itinerary.

## For culture: New York, Chicago and Santa Fe

**New York City**  
For sheer concentration, New York is difficult to match: Broadway, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, Lincoln Center and galleries across multiple boroughs. Its cultural advantage is variety as much as scale.

**Chicago, Illinois**  
Chicago combines major museums and celebrated architecture with theater, comedy and public art. The Art Institute of Chicago is a centerpiece, but an architectural river cruise may offer the most accessible introduction to the city’s creative history.

**Santa Fe, New Mexico**  
Smaller and slower-paced, Santa Fe offers a distinctive blend of Indigenous, Spanish Colonial and contemporary influences. Adobe architecture, museums, galleries and regional cuisine give the city an identity unlike that of any larger arts capital.

## For adventure: Honolulu, Denver and Portland

**Honolulu, Hawaii**  
Honolulu pairs an urban vacation with immediate access to the outdoors. Travelers can surf at Waikiki, hike Diamond Head, snorkel, paddle or venture around Oahu—all without sacrificing restaurants, shopping and nightlife.

**Denver, Colorado**  
The Mile High City serves as both a destination and a gateway. Its parks, bike paths and active culture suit a short urban stay, while the Rocky Mountains make hiking, skiing and scenic drives easy additions.

**Portland, Oregon**  
Portland is a natural base for travelers who want bike-friendly neighborhoods alongside forests, waterfalls and mountain scenery. The Columbia River Gorge and Mount Hood expand the possibilities for day trips.

## For families: Orlando, San Diego and Washington

**Orlando, Florida**  
Theme parks are the obvious draw, and few American cities offer as many large-scale family attractions in one place. The trade-off is crowds, so families should build downtime into multiday park schedules.

**San Diego, California**  
Beaches, mild weather, the San Diego Zoo and Balboa Park make San Diego a flexible choice for mixed-age groups. Families can alternate major attractions with low-key afternoons by the water.

**Washington, D.C.**  
The capital combines education and entertainment, often at relatively low cost. Smithsonian museums, monuments and the National Zoo provide enough variety for children, teenagers and adults.

## For romance: Charleston, Honolulu and San Francisco

**Charleston, South Carolina**  
Historic streets, garden courtyards, intimate inns and acclaimed restaurants make Charleston a natural couples’ getaway. Walking is part of the experience, especially in the older neighborhoods near the waterfront.

**Honolulu, Hawaii**  
Sunsets and beaches provide the obvious appeal, but couples can also find quieter moments away from Waikiki through coastal drives, hikes and stays elsewhere on Oahu.

**San Francisco, California**  
Cable cars, hilltop views, waterfront walks and neighborhood restaurants give San Francisco a cinematic quality. A trip can easily expand to include Sausalito, Muir Woods or the nearby wine country.

## The takeaway

The 2008 results did not identify one city that was best at everything. Instead, more than 600,000 votes produced a map of urban strengths: Austin for live music, New York for cultural abundance, Honolulu for outdoor escapes, Orlando for children and Charleston for a romantic weekend.

That may be the survey’s most enduring lesson. America’s favorite city depends first on what a traveler wants to do after arriving.
